did_you_know.text: Did you know? The expression "upon the Sheminith" is not explicitly explained in the psalm. It may refer to an eight-stringed musical instrument or to a particular melody, so its meaning is uncertain.
Did you know? The opening of the psalm presents a sense of moral decline: the faithful have disappeared, and faithfulness and loyalty are diminishing among people.
Did you know? The expression "with a double heart" describes speech that does not match a person’s true intentions: someone says one thing, but is not sincere in what they say.
Did you know? The psalmist asks the LORD to cut off not only lies, but also "flattering lips" and the tongue that speaks arrogantly—that is, flattery, deceit, and boastful speech.

Did you know? The wicked say, "With our tongues we will prevail," presenting the tongue as an instrument of power. The claim "Who is lord over us?" expresses rebellion and rejection of authority over them.

Did you know? In response to the plundering of the poor and the groans of the needy, the LORD declares, "Now I will arise." The rest of the verse can be understood in slightly different ways, but in every case it presents salvation as God’s response to the cry of the oppressed.
Did you know? The words of the LORD are compared to silver that has been thoroughly refined and purified. The image emphasizes their purity, reliability, and freedom from impurity or deceit.

Did you know? After describing the purity of the LORD’s words, the psalm gives a promise of protection: the LORD will keep and guard them. The verse emphasizes God’s protective presence in a generation described as surrounded by wickedness.

Did you know? The psalm does not end by describing a world in which the wicked have already disappeared. The wicked still walk about, and people must face a reality in which what is contemptible and base is given prominence.
